title: I Had a Lump Sum and Froze. All at Once or Spread It Out? Here’s What the Data Said.
summary: Taking a windfall all at once or spreading it out can change how much you keep after taxes and how your money grows.
body_markdown:
Getting a[lump sum](https://smartasset.com/retirement/lump-sum-payment) from an inheritance, bonus or home sale can feel like an irresistible windfall that puts a lot of money in your hands all at once. Yet, how much you actually get could be undercut by taxes, withdrawal timing and market drops. Here’s an example that compares taking one large amount or smaller amounts over a longer period.


## Which Will Pay You More: Lump Sum or Spreading It Out?


[Taxes on a windfall](https://smartasset.com/taxes/how-to-avoid-taxes-on-a-large-sum-of-money) depend on where the money comes from.[Inherited cash or investments](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/how-to-avoid-taxes-when-you-inherit-cash) typically aren’t subject to federal income tax, and only estates worth more than $15 million in 2026 ($15.48 million in 2027) may owe federal estate tax.1


An[inherited traditional IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/inherited-ira-rules-traditional-roth) works differently, since withdrawals generally count as taxable income. Most[non-spouse heirs](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/non-spouse-beneficiary-ira) must[empty the account within 10 years](https://smartasset.com/taxes/irs-inherited-ira-10-year-rule) of the original owner’s death, which leaves room to choose between one large distribution and several smaller ones.2


A work bonus, by comparison, offers less flexibility, because the full amount is taxed as income in the year you receive it. Employers may withhold[federal tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/income-taxes) on separately identified bonuses at a flat 22% rate on amounts up to $1 million, though other withholding methods can apply.3


[Selling a home](https://smartasset.com/taxes/taxes-on-selling-a-house) can be more forgiving, since part of the profit may be tax-free. Single filers can exclude up to $250,000 of gain and married couples up to $500,000 if they meet ownership and residency requirements.4


To get a clearer picture, let’s assume that you’re a single filer earning $75,000 a year and inherit a $500,000[traditional IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/traditional-ira) . After the[standard deduction](https://smartasset.com/taxes/standard-deduction) , your salary leaves $58,900 of taxable income in 2026 and $58,400 in 2027, so any IRA withdrawal is taxed starting in the 22% bracket. The table compares withdrawing the full balance at once with taking $50,000 annually over 10 years, using federal tax brackets for each year:5


Strategy Tax Year Tax Owed by Bracket Amount You Keep


$500,000 lump sum in one year 2026 22% × $46,800 = $10,296; 24% × $96,075 = $23,058; 32% × $54,450 = $17,424; 35% × $302,675 = $105,936; Total = $156,714 $500,000 − $156,714 = $343,286


$50,000 annual withdrawals over 10 years 2026 22% × $46,800 = $10,296; 24% × $3,200 = $768; Total = $11,064 a year × 10 = $110,640 $500,000 − $110,640 = $389,360


$500,000 lump sum in one year 2027 22% × $50,725 = $11,160; 24% × $99,200 = $23,808; 32% × $56,225 = $17,992; 35% × $293,850 = $102,848; Total = $155,807 $500,000 − $155,807 = $344,193


$50,000 annual withdrawals over 10 years 2027 22% × $50,000 = $11,000 a year × 10 = $110,000 $500,000 − $110,000 = $390,000


Spreading out the distributions would leave you with roughly $46,074 more under 2026 rules ($389,360 − $343,286) and about $45,807 more in 2027 ($390,000 − $344,193). A single $500,000 withdrawal pushes most of the inheritance into the 32% and 35% brackets. Each $50,000 withdrawal, on the other hand, stays almost entirely in the 22% bracket.


Leaving money in the IRA longer also keeps it invested, which could grow the balance if markets go up or shrink it if they fall before you take it out. This example assumes that tax brackets stay at 2026 or 2027 levels for all 10 years and exclude investment returns and[state income taxes](https://smartasset.com/taxes/what-to-know-about-state-taxes) .

## What Data Says About Investing a Windfall


A March 2026 study published in the journal of the American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) compared[investing a windfall](https://smartasset.com/investing/how-to-invest-large-sums-of-money) all at once with[dollar-cost averaging](https://smartasset.com/investing/dollar-cost-averaging) , which spreads the money into the market over time.6


The research used[S&P 500 returns](https://smartasset.com/investing/sp-500-average-annual-return) from January 1926 through September 2025. In each test, one investor put $1 million into the index on day one, while another invested $83,333 at the start of each month for a year.


The study then compared how each investor fared over rolling 20-year periods, along with periods that began when the market was at an all-time high. The table shows how often each approach came out ahead:


Scenario Lump Sum Came Out Ahead Dollar-Cost Averaging Came Out Ahead Average Result


All rolling 20-year periods 696 of 958 periods (73%) 262 of 958 periods (27%) Lump sum finished $398,770 ahead per $1 million invested


12-month periods starting at a market high 256 of 281 periods (91.1%) 25 of 281 periods (8.9%) Lump sum won by larger margins when it came out ahead


12-month periods not starting at a market high 440 of 677 periods (65%) 237 of 677 periods (35%) Lump sum won by larger margins when it came out ahead


The lump sum’s entire advantage was based on the first year, when that money was fully invested while the other investor was still phasing in. That head start averaged $59,732 per $1 million after 12 months and grew to $398,770 over the following 19 years as both portfolios tracked the market.


Dollar-cost averaging still came out ahead in about a quarter of the 20-year periods. Even then, its average winning margin of $725,583 trailed the lump sum’s average winning margin of $822,017.


## Which Should You Pick: Lump Sum or Spreading It Out?


While AAII data favored investing a lump sum all at once, its research was limited to how quickly money enters the market. Spreading withdrawals may still offer tax advantages. If an early drop leads you to sell, investing in equal amounts over several months could help you stay on track, even if it means giving up some potential gains.
